title: The support desk plan
scenario:
You lead customer support at a 30-person company that sells coffee machines online. The support inbox gets about 400 emails a week. Your manager wrote a plan to use AI in the team and asks you to check it before it starts.

Use the exhibit. The company, the plan and the emails are made up for this case. Facts about the tools are from the Claude docs and the OpenAI docs, October 2026.
exhibit:
AI SUPPORT PLAN (made up)

  1. Sorting: AI reads each new email and gives
     it one type: "Order", "Machine", "Other".
     Nobody has written down what each type means.
  2. Replies: AI drafts a reply to each email.
     An agent reads it, edits it and sends it.
  3. Website chat: a bot answers questions on
     returns by itself, writing each answer
     fresh. We have 12 approved help articles.
  4. A "Report a problem" link under the chat
     sends reports to an inbox. Owner: none yet.

AI DRAFT REPLY (for item 2)
  Customer: "My machine leaks after 3 weeks."
  Draft: "So sorry! We'll send you a brand-new
  machine today, and we'll add a free year of
  coffee beans for the trouble."

RETURNS POLICY (real for this company)
  Faults in the first 2 years: we repair the
  machine for free, or replace the faulty part.

questions.prompt: Look at the draft reply in item 2. What should the agent do before sending it?

options.text: Send it as it is, since a kind reply keeps the customer happy
options.explanation: Kind words are fine, but the draft promises things the policy does not give. The customer will hold the company to them.

options.text: Cut the apology, because an apology admits the fault is ours
options.explanation: The apology is not the problem. The problem is the promise of a new machine and free beans.

options.text: Rewrite the offer to match the policy: a free repair or a new part
options.explanation: Right. The Claude docs say a support agent should not make promises it is not authorized to make, and replies should match company policy and known facts.

options.text: Keep the new machine, but remove the free year of coffee beans
options.explanation: A new machine is still not what the policy offers. Only a person allowed to change the policy can promise that.

questions.prompt: Item 1 sorts emails into "Order", "Machine" and "Other". What does the Claude ticket routing guide say makes this kind of sorting work well?

options.text: Using as few types as possible, so the tool rarely has to choose
options.explanation: Fewer types do not help if nobody knows what they mean. The guide links good routing to well-defined types.

options.text: Types that are clearly defined, so each one has a written meaning
options.explanation: Right. The guide ties good routing to how clearly each category is defined.

options.text: Letting the tool make up new types whenever it finds a new email
options.explanation: New types made up on the fly are not defined. The team would not know where emails go.

options.text: Sorting only short emails, because long emails confuse the tool
options.explanation: The guide does not limit sorting to short emails. The weak point here is the undefined types.

questions.prompt: Item 3 has the chat bot write each return answer fresh. What does the OpenAI safety page suggest instead?

options.text: Answer from the best-matching approved help article where it can
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI docs say returning a matching existing support article can be safer than writing a new answer from scratch.

options.text: Write longer answers, so the customer gets every detail at once
options.explanation: Length does not make an answer true. The page points to answers built from checked material.

options.text: Turn off the help articles, so the bot is not limited by old text
options.explanation: That is the opposite of the advice. Approved articles are the checked material the bot should use.

options.text: Let the bot answer only at night, when no agents are on shift
options.explanation: The time of day does not change the risk. The answers still come from nowhere checked.

questions.prompt: Item 4 says the "Report a problem" inbox has no owner. What should the plan say?

options.text: The bot reads the reports and fixes its own answers each night
options.explanation: The OpenAI docs want a person, not the tool that made the problem, to watch the reports.

options.text: Nothing, because few customers ever use a report link at all
options.explanation: Even a few reports can point to a wrong answer many people got. Someone must read them.

options.text: Reports are deleted after a week, so the inbox never gets full
options.explanation: Deleting reports nobody read does not fix anything. A person needs to read and answer them.

options.text: A named person reads the reports and answers them as needed
options.explanation: Right. The OpenAI safety page says a person should watch the way customers report problems, and reply where needed.
